newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Yachts for Bulgaria's rich brighten gloomy outlook.
newsitem.headline: Yachts for Bulgaria's rich brighten gloomy outlook.

text.p: While many Bulgarians struggle to pay electricity bills or buy food, a lucky few are racing to snap up the latest lines in luxury yachts.
The booming luxury yacht market highlights the gap between rich and poor, seen through most of former communist Euorpe and likely to play a role in presidential elections scheduled for Sunday.
"Bulgaria is the cheapest place to shop for yachts," sports equipment importer Sasho Sulkoff told Reuters.
Bulgaria's crumbling banks, soaring prices and power cuts and shortages make it an unlikely market for his 15-metre (50-foot) motor boats, but Sulkoff is optimistic.
"There are thousands of affluent people in this country and I personally know many of them," he said.
"A $60,000 luxurious yacht is a far better acquisition than a luxury car which costs three to four times more," he said.

Mercedes and BMW cars on Bulgarian streets have become a controversial symbol of the transition to democracy and the market economy. Many of their owners' banks are in receivership and others have fled to avoid paying million-dollar credits.

The vast majority of Bulgarians are gripped by unprecedented economic crisis. Sunday's polls offer them a choice between the governing Socialists or accelerated free enterprise offered by the opposition.

Latest opinion polls show 32.5 percent support for opposition candidate Petar Stoyanov, 21.5 percent for the Socialist Ivan Marazov, and colourful politician George Ganchev close behind with 18.5 percent.

Delays in implementing economic reform have brought Bulgaria to the verge of bankruptcy, but at the same time lax banking legislation has created so-called "credit millionaires". Credits have been extended without clear controls, offering fast access to loose cash for sometimes less-than-scrupulous businessmen.
Another wealthy group are the "wrestlers", former sportsmen who have put their brawn in crime working under the cover of 100 security firms.
Professional sportsmen, local petrol traders and customs officers are also Sulkoff's potential clients.
"There is lot of money in this country, but it is unevenly distributed," said Sulkoff.
